title: How the internet agrees on where things are
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what an autonomous system is, describe how routes propagate between networks, and say why a single misconfigured announcement can take a service off the internet.

blocks.text: The routing lesson showed a machine choosing a next hop from its own table. That leaves a question: where do the routers at the top get their tables? Nobody assigns them. Networks tell each other what they can reach, and the protocol they use for that is BGP. It is the reason the internet works, and the reason it occasionally does not.
The internet is a network of networks

Each independently operated network — an internet provider, a university, a large company, a cloud platform — is an autonomous system with its own number. Inside one, the operator chooses how to route. Between them, they exchange announcements: 'these address ranges are reachable through me'.

rows: Find the shortest or cheapest path

blocks.title: Between networks, the shortest path is not the goal
blocks.text: Inside your own network you want the fastest route. Between networks, an operator prefers the path that costs them least, or that a contract requires, or that a peering agreement favours — which may be longer. This is the single most important thing to understand about internet routing: it follows business relationships at least as much as geography, which is why traffic between two cities in one country sometimes leaves the country and comes back.

items: A network announces to its neighbours: 'I can reach 203.0.113.0/24'
Each neighbour that accepts it adds its own identifier to the path and passes it on
A router receiving several announcements for the same range picks one according to its own policy
The chosen one is installed in the routing table, and the packet-forwarding decision from the earlier lesson uses it
Withdrawals propagate the same way when a route disappears

blocks.text: The path each announcement carries serves two purposes: it lets a receiver compare routes, and it prevents loops — a network that sees its own identifier already in a path rejects that announcement, because accepting it would create a circle.

In its original design, BGP has no way to verify that an announcement is legitimate. If a network announces a range it does not own, its neighbours may believe it, and traffic for that range starts flowing to the wrong place. This has happened repeatedly, both by accident — a configuration typo — and deliberately.

rows: A network passes on routes it should have kept to itself
Traffic takes a wildly indirect path and slows down or drops
A network announces addresses it does not hold
Traffic goes to the wrong operator entirely
A hijacker announces a smaller prefix than the real owner
It wins, because longest prefix always wins
A network stops announcing its own range

blocks.title: The longest-prefix rule works against you here
blocks.text: The routing lesson established that the most specific route always wins. In global routing that means an operator announcing a /24 out-competes the legitimate holder announcing the /16 that contains it — everywhere that accepts the announcement. The rule is not a bug; it is the same rule that makes routing tractable. It simply has no notion of who is entitled to announce what, which is what the protections below add.
What is being done about it

items: Address holders can publish signed statements saying which networks may announce their ranges, and receivers can check announcements against them
Operators filter what they accept from customers, rather than believing everything
Public route-collector projects make announcements visible, so a hijack is noticed in minutes rather than hours
Encryption limits the damage: traffic diverted through an attacker is still unreadable if it is properly encrypted end to end

blocks.text: That last point connects to the ARP lesson. Both protocols answer 'where should this traffic go' and neither authenticates the answer. In both cases the practical defence is the same: assume the path may be hostile, and encrypt so that a diverted path is an availability problem rather than a confidentiality one.
Why this matters if you do not run a network

items: It explains outages you cannot fix: sometimes a service is unreachable from your provider and fine from another
It explains latency that geography does not: traffic follows contracts, not straight lines
It is the mechanism behind large-scale anycast, where the same address is announced from many locations and each user reaches the nearest
It is why 'the internet is down' is almost always 'a path is down' — the destination is usually fine

blocks.title: Look at global routing from outside
steps: Find which network an address belongs to: whois -h whois.cymru.com ' -v 1.1.1.1'    if available
Run: traceroute -A 1.1.1.1     — the -A flag annotates hops with their network numbers where supported
Count how many distinct networks your traffic crosses to reach a well-known service
Compare with a service in another country and note whether the count grows
Open a public looking-glass or route-collector website and search for a well-known prefix
Note how many different paths exist to the same destination
Read one recent public report of a routing incident and identify which failure type from the table it was
Explain why an encrypted connection limited its impact
blocks.expected: A concrete sense of how few networks separate you from most services, and one real incident you can classify. Being able to say 'that was a more-specific hijack, and it won because longest prefix wins' is the level of understanding this lesson is aiming for.

cheatsheet: The internet is independently operated networks exchanging reachability announcements
Each network is an autonomous system with its own number
Inside a network, routing optimises for speed; between networks, it follows policy and contracts
An announcement carries the path it travelled, which enables comparison and prevents loops
BGP as originally designed does not verify that an announcement is legitimate
Route leak, prefix hijack, more-specific hijack, withdrawal — four distinct failure modes
Longest prefix always wins, so a more specific announcement beats the legitimate broader one
Defences: signed authorisations, customer filtering, public monitoring, end-to-end encryption
Traffic follows business relationships, which is why latency does not always match geography

checkpoint.prompt: Why might traffic between two cities in the same country leave the country and come back?

choices.B: Routing between networks follows policy and contracts rather than geography

checkpoint.explanation: Inside a single network the goal is the shortest path. Between networks it is the path the operator's agreements and costs favour, which may be much longer physically.

checkpoint.prompt: An operator announces a /24 inside a range legitimately held by someone else announcing a /16. What happens?

choices.A: The announcement is ignored as invalid
choices.B: The /24 wins wherever it is accepted, because the most specific route always wins

checkpoint.explanation: The longest-prefix rule from the routing lesson applies globally, and it has no notion of entitlement. That is precisely what signed authorisations and customer filtering exist to address.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the path carried in an announcement do, besides letting receivers compare routes?

choices.B: It prevents loops — a network that sees its own identifier in a path rejects the announcement
choices.D: It sets the packet's hop limit

checkpoint.explanation: Loop prevention is structural. Note what it does not do: it carries no proof that any network on it was entitled to announce the range.

checkpoint.prompt: Traffic to your service is hijacked and routed through an attacker. Your connections use TLS. What is the impact?

choices.B: Mainly availability and latency — the traffic is diverted but remains unreadable without a certificate the client accepts
choices.D: TLS prevents the hijack from happening

checkpoint.explanation: Same shape as the ARP lesson: the routing layer cannot authenticate, so encryption converts a confidentiality problem into an availability one. It does not prevent the diversion.
